Glasgow University Court : Retirement of Professors.? 
At a recent meeting of the Glasgow University Court the 
retirement of two of Glasgow's best known teachers, Sir 
Robert Muir, Professor of Pathology, and Dr. T. K. Monro, 
238 
Current Topics 
Regius Professor of the Practice of Medicine, was intimated. Sir 
Robert Muir retires on 30th September, and Dr. T. K. Monro 
on 30th June. 
The University's loss will be great. 
Sir Robert Muir is one of the greatest living pathologists, and 
the extraordinary number of his former assistants who hold 
professorial appointments bears testimony to his wonderful gifts. 
Muir and Ritchie's " Manual of Bacteriology" is the standard 
work on the subject, and Muir's " Manual of Pathology 
" has few 
equals. 
Professor T. K. Monro is best known by his text-book on 
Medicine, which is used by students in all parts of the country, 
but he has by no means confined his activities to Medicine alone. 
His great erudition has been the envy of all who have come into 
contact with him. A book published by him in 1933, "The 
Physician as Man of Letters, Science, and Action," is but one 
example of his great versatility.

Scottish Nurses' Club: Annual Meeting.?The eighteenth 
annual meeting of the Scottish Nurses' Club was held on 28th 
March, 1936, in the Club premises at 203 Bath Street, Glasgow. 
The Marchioness of Ailsa, president of the Club, occupied the 
chair. The gathering represented a large number of members of 
the nursing profession and their friends. The various reports 
were submitted and satisfaction was expressed at the successful 
result obtained, indicating the continuance of careful and wise

management. The number of members on the roll at the end of 
the working year was 267, showing an increase of new members 
over the previous year. The club rooms were still maintaining 
their useful purpose in providing accommodation for the various 
social functions held throughout the year. The Club had 
welcomed visitors from Australia, New Zealand, Canada, and 
South and West Africa, and it was especially gratifying to know 
that by means of this "open door," and the comforts afforded by 
so valuable a 
" home," its privileges were appreciated in a farreaching and ever-widening sphere. 
Mrs. Strong, formerly Matron of the Royal Infirmary, spoke a 
few words of good cheer to the nurses. Miss Nunn, at present 
home on a visit from China, gave a stimulating account of the 
work carried on amongst the Chinese in Shantung, in association 
with the Union of University Missions, and commended it to the 
sympathy of those in the homeland. 
Lady Ailsa, in gracious terms, expressed her good wishes to the 
nurses regarding the realization of their hopes for the future of 
the Scottish Nurses' Club. 
Hazelwood House.?The annual meeting of the Committee 
of the Nurses' Memorial to King Edward VII in Scotland, 
Hazelwood House, Dumbreck, was held at Hazelwood House, on 
26th March, 1936, Sir John Cargill, Bt., in the chair. The 
Reports by the House and Finance Committees were submitted 
and their adoption moved by Sir James Macfarlane, D.L., LL.D. 
The House Committee's report disclosed that the Home was full 
with its complement of twenty-six nurses, and that twenty-two 
were on the waiting list, but mentioned that a number on the 
waiting list were still actively engaged in their profession and 
would not apply for admission until they felt unable to continue 
nursing.

The Accounts disclosed that the revenue exceeded the 
expenditure by the sum of ?28 3s. Sir James Macfarlane, in 
moving the adoption of the Accounts, referred to the fact that 
other Institutions with which he was connected were, as a rule,

faced with deficits at the end of the year and had constantly to 
appeal for increased subscriptions, but that Hazelwood House 
found itself in the unique position of being self-contained in that 
respect. He referred to the difficulty nurses had in making 
provision for the time when they were no longer able to work, 
and that the larger hospitals were taking up superannuation 
schemes. 
Lady Gardiner, as president of the Home, also spoke, and 
referred to the good work done by the Matron, Miss Valentine. 
The existing Committees and Office-Bearers were re-elected 
with the addition of Miss Craig, the Matron of the Western 
Infirmary, whose name was added to the House and Executive 
Committees. 
National Radium Commission.?In the Commission's Sixth 
Annual Report it is stated that several of the most responsible 
and progressive centres require more radium for carrying out 
their work, as the present tendency is for radium to be used in 
mass units. The Commission feels that it is highly desirable to 
increase the number of large units to work under organized 
arrangements, so that the usual prolonged period for assessing 
the full value of radium therapy may be reduced. 
Since National radium became available six years ago, the 
Commission have had 20 grammes put at their disposal and they 
now believe that at least a further 20 grammes could be used on 
the following lines :? 
1. In a form similar to that already handed over to the 
Commission to enable?(a) Existing centres to treat the population of larger areas, and, or (b) The number of centres to be 
increased. 
2. In the form of one gramme or larger units. 
The Commission also find that most centres keep all available 
beds occupied by radium patients, so that to increase their loans 
of radium would be of small value unless provision for more beds 
were made.

Maternal Mortality : British Medical Association's 
Report.?The problems associated with maternal mortality have 
been investigated by various committees of the British Medical 
Association and the conclusions have been, that normal confinements and those showing only minor departures from the normal

can be more safely conducted at home than in hospital, and also 
that the provision of hospital beds for maternity cases, without 
careful selection, had resulted in an appreciable increase in 
maternal mortality. They hold that the State, by some means 
or other, should make available to a woman during the period of 
maternity certain medical requirements, namely :?(1) Medical 
supervision throughout by the doctor of her choice, with specialist 
and hospital aid where needed; (2) Efficient nursing and advice 
by a skilled midwife or maternity nurse of her choice; (3) Provision of help in the house during the period of her actual 
incapacity; (4) Supply of dressings, special apparatus, or means 
of transport when required.

Revue M?dicale Franc;aise. " Journees Medicales de 
Paris." Third Session, 26th to 30th June, 1937. The standing 
committee of the "Journees Medicales de Paris" has decided to 
arrange during the course of the 1937 International Exhibition 
a course of Meetings on the general lines of those of the first 
two series (1926 and 1929). These Meetings will bring together 
doctors in Civil practice, doctors of the Army and Air Force, 
pharmacists, veterinary surgeons, biologists, physicists and 
chemists?both French and foreign. 
The organization of the usual exhibition will be undertaken 
as before by the " Comite fran^ais des Expositions," under the 
direction of Monsieur Jean Faure.

The mornings will be given up as usual to practical

demonstrations in the Civil or Military Hospitals as well as in 
Schools and Institutes of Biology; all branches of medical work 
will be touched on. 
The afternoon Meetings will be devoted to practical study of 
the following subject:?"Hormones and Endocrine Therapeutics." 
First day?Pituitary gland; Second day?Glands of the Genital
